title: Undo It, Do It Again
objectives: I can use the prefix un- to understand words that mean not.
I can use the prefix re- to understand words that mean again.
I can take apart a long word to find the prefix and the base word.
I can write sentences that use un- and re- words correctly.
rationale: After four meaning-based units, this is the first affix unit and gives students a tool for unfamiliar words. Grades 1 and 2 taught short un- and re- words such as unkind and redo; here the words are longer and less obvious: five un- adjectives (unusual, uneasy, unfamiliar, unlikely, unaware) and five re- verbs (reunite, rearrange, reappear, reconsider, reassemble). Each word splits cleanly into a prefix and a base the student already knows, so the routine is the same every time: cover the prefix, say the base, then say what the prefix changes. The unit warns that not every un- or re- begins a prefix, which sets up the careful word-part work of grade 4.

words.def: Different from what is normal or expected.
words.ex: The unusual shape of the cloud looked like a dragon.
words.ex2: It is unusual to see snow in this town in October.
words.nonExample: A dog barking at the mail carrier is not unusual.

apps.academic: A scientist notices an unusual result and asks why it happened.
apps.spoken: That is an unusual hat; I have never seen one like it.
apps.writing: Use unusual to tell readers that something is out of the ordinary.

cloze.s: A bright green bird landed on the porch, and the ___ sight made everyone stop talking.

cloze2.s: Because Dad never cooks breakfast, a hot pancake on the table was an ___ surprise.

misuse.s: It is unusual to see the sun come up every morning, because it happens every single day.
misuse.why: Unusual means not normal; something that happens every day is normal.

visual.alt: A bright green bird on a porch rail with a question mark above it.

words.def: Worried or uncomfortable, as if something is wrong.
words.ex: Mia felt uneasy walking alone through the dark parking lot.
words.ex2: An uneasy quiet filled the room after the loud crash.
words.nonExample: Feeling calm and happy on a sunny afternoon is not feeling uneasy.

apps.academic: A character who feels uneasy senses that something may go wrong.
apps.spoken: I felt uneasy when the lights flickered.
apps.writing: Use uneasy for a mild worry that does not have a clear cause yet.

cloze.s: Something about the empty house made the babysitter feel ___, so she kept the lights on.

cloze2.s: The kitten gave an ___ glance at the barking dog and backed under the couch.

misuse.s: She felt uneasy and perfectly calm, with no worry at all.
misuse.why: Uneasy means worried; being perfectly calm is the opposite.

visual.alt: A worried child sitting alone in a dim room.

words.def: Not known to you; new or strange.
words.ex: The unfamiliar streets made the new student nervous.
words.ex2: An unfamiliar voice answered the phone.
words.nonExample: Your own bedroom is not unfamiliar to you.

apps.academic: In stories, an unfamiliar place can make a character feel lost.
apps.spoken: This song is unfamiliar to me; can you play it again?
apps.writing: Use unfamiliar for people, places, or words you have not met before.

cloze.s: The traveler studied the map in the ___ city and tried to find the train station.

cloze2.s: When the teacher read a long, ___ word, the class guessed its meaning from the sentence.

misuse.s: The unfamiliar path was the one he had walked every day of his life.
misuse.why: Unfamiliar means not known to you; a path you walk every day is well known.

visual.alt: A map and a compass lying on a strange street.

words.def: Not expected to happen; probably not true.
words.ex: It is unlikely that it will snow on a hot summer day.
words.ex2: The team's win seemed unlikely until the very last minute.
words.nonExample: The sun rising tomorrow morning is not unlikely.

apps.academic: In math and science, an unlikely event has a low chance of happening.
apps.spoken: It's unlikely that I'll finish before lunch.
apps.writing: Use unlikely when something has only a small chance of happening.

cloze.s: With only one cloud in the sky, rain was ___ for the picnic.

cloze2.s: It seemed ___ that the tiny team could beat the champions, but they did.

misuse.s: It is unlikely that the sun will rise tomorrow, because that almost always happens.
misuse.why: Unlikely means not expected; the sunrise is certain.

visual.alt: A single die beside a small cloud on a clear day.

words.def: Not knowing about something that is happening.
words.ex: Lena was unaware that her friends were planning a surprise party.
words.ex2: The campers were unaware of the storm moving toward them.
words.nonExample: Someone who sees the warning sign and stops is not unaware.

apps.academic: A character who is unaware of danger may walk right into trouble.
apps.spoken: I was unaware that the bell had rung.
apps.writing: Use unaware when a character does not know a fact that the reader knows.

cloze.s: The boy kept reading, ___ that the bus had already left the stop.

cloze2.s: Lost in her music, Dana was ___ of the rain until her shoes were soaked.

misuse.s: He was unaware that the bee was on his arm, even though he stared at it and screamed.
misuse.why: Unaware means not knowing; staring at the bee shows he knows about it.

visual.alt: A girl wearing headphones, smiling, while rain falls around her.

words.def: To come together again after being apart.
words.ex: The lost puppy was finally reunited with its family.
words.ex2: The two friends hoped to reunite after summer vacation.
words.nonExample: Moving to a new town and never seeing your friends is not reuniting.

apps.academic: In history, families were sometimes reunited after a long journey.
apps.spoken: I can't wait to reunite with my cousins this summer.
apps.writing: Use reunite for people or animals coming back together after time apart.

cloze.s: After months at sea, the sailor was thrilled to ___ with his family, and everyone cried with joy.

cloze2.s: The shelter worked hard to find the lost dog's owner so the two could ___ quickly.

misuse.s: The friends reunited for the first time, and they had never met before in their lives.
misuse.why: Reunite means to come together again; people who never met cannot reunite.

visual.alt: A dog running into the arms of a smiling family.

words.frame: I would like to reunite with ___.

words.def: To put things in a different order or place.
words.ex: We rearranged the desks into a circle for the class discussion.
words.ex2: Mom rearranged the furniture so the piano would fit by the window.
words.nonExample: Leaving everything exactly where it was is not rearranging.

apps.academic: In math, you can rearrange numbers to make them easier to add.
apps.spoken: Let's rearrange the seats so everyone can see.
apps.writing: Use rearrange when the same things are placed in a new order.

cloze.s: To fit the new bookshelf, the family had to ___ the whole living room.

cloze2.s: Ravi will ___ the letters in the word 'lemon' to spell a new word on the game board.

misuse.s: She rearranged the toys by leaving every single one in the exact same spot.
misuse.why: Rearrange means to put things in a new order; leaving them in the same place is not rearranging.

visual.alt: Chairs being moved into a new circle with a circular arrow.

words.def: To come into view again after being gone.
words.ex: The sun reappeared after the storm clouds blew away.
words.ex2: After a week, the missing cat reappeared on the porch.
words.nonExample: A coin that stays hidden forever has not reappeared.

apps.academic: In science, the moon seems to reappear in a new shape each night.
apps.spoken: My lost sock reappeared in the dryer.
apps.writing: Use reappear for a person, animal, or thing that comes back into sight.

cloze.s: After the magician covered the coin with a cloth, it began to ___ in his other hand.

cloze2.s: We waited by the window for the rainbow to ___ when the clouds moved away again.

misuse.s: The ghost reappeared for the first time in all of history and had never been seen before.
misuse.why: Reappear means to come back into view; something never seen before cannot reappear.

visual.alt: The sun coming out from behind a cloud.

words.def: To think about something again and maybe change your mind.
words.ex: After talking with her friends, Lina decided to reconsider her answer.
words.ex2: The coach agreed to reconsider the rule after the team asked politely.
words.nonExample: Refusing to listen to anyone is not reconsidering.

apps.academic: A good scientist will reconsider an idea when new evidence appears.
apps.spoken: Can you reconsider and let me stay up a little later?
apps.writing: Use reconsider for thinking again about a choice, plan, or answer.

cloze.s: When the new facts came out, the judge asked everyone to ___ their first opinion.

cloze2.s: Mom said she would ___ her no if I finished my chores without being asked.

misuse.s: He reconsidered by refusing to think about the plan a second time.
misuse.why: Reconsider means to think again; refusing to think again is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child with a thought bubble and a circular arrow.

words.def: To put the parts together a second time.
words.ex: Dad reassembled the bike after painting each piece.
words.ex2: The students reassembled the broken model with glue and patience.
words.nonExample: Throwing the parts in the trash is not reassembling.

apps.academic: A mechanic may take an engine apart and then reassemble it.
apps.spoken: I took my toy apart, and now I have to reassemble it.
apps.writing: Use reassemble when the parts of something are put back together.

cloze.s: After the careful cleaning, the clockmaker began to ___ the tiny gears inside the clock.

cloze2.s: The vase fell and broke, so the girl tried to ___ the pieces with tape.

misuse.s: He reassembled the model by smashing each piece into dust with a hammer.
misuse.why: Reassemble means to put parts together again; smashing them is the opposite.

visual.alt: A bicycle in pieces next to a wrench.

words.frame: It is hard to reassemble ___ because ___.

passage.title: The Castle Puzzle
paras: On a rainy Saturday, Kai and his grandfather opened a box that held an unusual puzzle. The picture showed a castle, but the pieces were shaped like leaves. Kai felt uneasy. The shapes looked unfamiliar, and he thought it was unlikely that he could finish.

They worked for an hour. Then Kai noticed that one piece was missing. "Maybe we should reconsider," he said. "Let's try a different puzzle." Grandpa smiled. "First, let's rearrange the pieces by color," he said.
Kai was unaware that his little sister, Nia, had taken the blue sky piece to use as a boat in the bathtub. That night she gave it back, and the piece reappeared on the table.

Then Dad bumped the board, and the castle fell apart. "We will reassemble it tomorrow," said Grandpa. Kai laughed. The puzzle had helped to reunite the whole family around the table, and no one wanted to stop.

qs.why: The leaf-shaped pieces were new to Kai, so the shapes were not known to him.

qs.q: Why did Kai say, "Maybe we should reconsider"?
choices: He wanted to think again about the puzzle because a piece was missing.
He wanted to give the puzzle to Nia.
He was angry at his grandfather.
qs.why: Kai noticed a missing piece and thought they might need a different plan.

choices: Nia had taken the blue piece.
qs.why: Unaware means not knowing, and the text says Kai did not know where the blue piece went.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Puzzles are too hard for children.
A little sister should never touch a puzzle.
A family worked together to solve a puzzle and fix a problem.
qs.why: The passage shows the family working on the puzzle, finding the missing piece, and planning to continue.

write.prompt: Write about a time you took something apart, rearranged something, or tried again. Use two un- or re- words from this unit.
write.frame: I felt ___ when I had to ___ again because ___.

study.task: Cover un- or re- at the start of a unit word and say the base word. Then say what the whole word means: not ___, or ___ again. Choose two words and use each in a sentence.

Write a sentence that uses unlikely and tells what is probably not going to happen.
Write a sentence about something you would rearrange in your classroom.
Write a sentence about someone who had to reconsider. What new fact changed the thinking?

combine.model: The lost puppy was reunited with its family.

given: Mia was alone in the parking lot.
combine.model: Mia felt uneasy because she was alone in the dark parking lot.

discuss: How does knowing the prefix help you with a word you have never seen?
What is the difference between feeling uneasy and feeling scared?
When is it smart to reconsider a decision?
produce.explain: Explain how the prefix re- changes the meaning of reappear. Give an example from your life.

argue.prompt: Claim: It is better to reconsider a choice than to stick with it. Do you agree or disagree? Give two reasons.
argue.frame: I agree (or disagree) that ___ because ___. Another reason is ___.

constructed.prompt: Write two sentences about a trip to a new place. Use unusual and unfamiliar and tell what the traveler saw.
constructed.model: The streets in the new town were unfamiliar, and the traveler used a map. She saw an unusual building shaped like a boat.

constructed.prompt: Explain the difference between rearrange and reassemble. Use both words and an example for each.
look: explains that rearrange changes order and reassemble puts parts together
constructed.model: When I rearrange my desk, I move things into a new order. When I reassemble a toy, I put its parts back together.

teacher.overview: Students use the prefixes un- (not) and re- (again) to understand ten longer words. They split each word into prefix and base, read a narrative where the words appear naturally, and write sentences that apply the meaning of the prefix.

notes.va.unusual.adj: Unusual = un- (not) + usual. Cover un- and say the base. Ask students to name one unusual thing they saw this week.
notes.va.uneasy.adj: Uneasy = un- + easy, where easy means comfortable. Distinguish from scared: uneasy is a smaller, quieter worry. Link to the unit 1 word timid.
notes.va.unfamiliar.adj: Unfamiliar = un- + familiar. Connect to reading: unfamiliar words are the ones students use context clues to solve.
notes.va.unlikely.adj: Unlikely sits on the likelihood ladder between impossible and possible. Ask students to rank four events on the ladder.
notes.va.unaware.adj: Unaware is followed by 'that' or 'of'. Link to the idea of dramatic irony in a very simple way: the reader knows something the character does not.
notes.va.reunite.v: Reunite = re- (again) + unite (join). A reunion is the noun. Ask students about a time they were reunited with someone.
notes.va.rearrange.v: Rearrange keeps the same items but changes where they are. Use letter cards to rearrange 'stop' into 'pots' and 'tops'.
notes.va.reappear.v: Reappear = re- + appear. The opposite is disappear. Show a hidden object and bring it back as a quick demonstration.
notes.va.reconsider.v: Reconsider means thinking again, not always changing your mind. Ask students to name a time new information made them think again.
notes.va.reassemble.v: Reassemble = re- + assemble. Show a simple object taken apart, then put back together, and describe each step with a re- word.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see the word unfamiliar. I cover un- and I see familiar. Familiar means well known. The prefix un- means not, so unfamiliar means not well known. Now I check it in the sentence about the new streets. It makes sense.'
discuss: Which un- word in this unit would a character use when something feels strange?
Why can you rearrange without reassembling?
misconceptions: Every word that begins with un- or re- uses that prefix (for example, under and read).
Re- always means again, even in words such as recess.
Un- means the opposite of everything.
Rearrange and reassemble mean the same thing.
extend: Sort a list of words into 'has the prefix' and 'only looks like it has the prefix' (uncle, until, recess, real, reread).
Make a poster of three un- or re- words with the base word circled in color.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Two days later, give students three new un- and re- words to split. Revisit timid, rustle, and stammer by asking them to describe a scene that uses an un- word and one of those words.

frames: The word ___ has the prefix ___, which means ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says a base word such as easy or arrange. Partner B adds un- or re- when it makes a real word and says what the new word means.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (inquieto, desconocido, inconsciente, reordenar, volver a armar) are not reviewed by a native speaker.
Check the study note that not every word starting with un- or re- uses the prefix (for example, uncle and recess) before using it in a lesson.
Reappear lists disappear as an antonym and a family word; confirm this is clear for third graders.
